units.title: Requirements and Planning
units.tip: Good software starts with clear requirements that define what the system must do. Understanding requirements prevents building the wrong thing. Gathering requirements involves talking to stakeholders and documenting what they need.

exercises.question: What are software requirements?
exercises.answer: Detailed specifications of what a software system must do
exercises.explain: Requirements describe the system's features, behavior, and constraints. They come from stakeholders and define success criteria for the project.
choices: Detailed specifications of what a software system must do
The hardware needed to run the software

exercises.question: What is a functional requirement?
exercises.answer: A description of what the system must do
exercises.explain: Functional requirements describe capabilities like features and behavior: 'Users must be able to log in' or 'The system must calculate totals.' They define features.
choices: Whether the system uses a database
A description of what the system must do
How fast the system must run
How much memory the system uses

exercises.question: What is a non-functional requirement?
exercises.answer: A constraint on how the system operates
exercises.explain: Non-functional requirements specify quality attributes like performance, security, and reliability: 'The system must respond in under 1 second' or 'Data must be encrypted.' They constrain behavior.
choices: A constraint on how the system operates
A feature the system must provide

exercises.question: What is a user story in requirements gathering?
exercises.answer: A brief description of a feature from a user's perspective
exercises.explain: User stories follow the format: 'As a [role], I want [feature] so that [benefit].' They communicate requirements in everyday language.
choices: A brief description of a feature from a user's perspective
A fictional narrative in the application

exercises.question: Why is it important to clarify requirements before coding?
exercises.answer: Fixing requirement mistakes early costs far less than fixing them after implementation
exercises.explain: Discovering a missing requirement after coding can require rewriting entire systems. Clarity upfront prevents wasted work.
choices: Fixing requirement mistakes early costs far less than fixing them after implementation
It is not important; coding can start immediately

exercises.question: What is project planning in software engineering?
exercises.answer: Breaking down work into tasks, estimating effort, and scheduling
exercises.explain: Planning defines what needs to be done, how long it will take, and who will do it. It creates a roadmap for the project.
choices: Writing all the code before starting
Breaking down work into tasks, estimating effort, and scheduling

exercises.question: What is estimation in project planning?
exercises.answer: Predicting how long tasks will take and how many resources are needed
exercises.explain: Estimation forecasts effort, cost, and timeline. It is never exact, but good estimates prevent overruns.
choices: Recording how long work actually took
Predicting how long tasks will take and how many resources are needed

exercises.question: What is the 'cone of uncertainty'?
exercises.answer: The uncertainty in estimates narrows as a project progresses
exercises.explain: Early estimates are very uncertain, with errors that can be large in either direction. As details emerge and work is done, estimates become more accurate.
choices: The uncertainty in estimates narrows as a project progresses

exercises.question: What is a Gantt chart?
exercises.answer: A visual timeline showing tasks, duration, and dependencies
exercises.explain: Gantt charts display project tasks as horizontal bars over time. They show which tasks depend on others and when each must complete.
choices: A visual timeline showing tasks, duration, and dependencies

exercises.question: What is scope creep in a project?
exercises.answer: Uncontrolled expansion of project requirements beyond the original plan
exercises.explain: Scope creep happens when new features are added without adjusting timeline or resources. It causes delays and budget overruns.
choices: Uncontrolled expansion of project requirements beyond the original plan
The natural progress of a project

units.title: Version Control and Collaboration
units.tip: Version control systems track changes to code over time. They allow multiple developers to work together without losing changes. Git is the most widely used one.

exercises.question: What is version control?
exercises.answer: A system that tracks changes to files over time and allows reverting to earlier versions
exercises.explain: Version control records who changed what and when. It enables collaboration and provides a safety net if changes break something.
choices: A way to manage software releases
A system that tracks changes to files over time and allows reverting to earlier versions

exercises.question: What is a repository in version control?
exercises.answer: The central storage location for all project files and their history
exercises.explain: A repository (or repo) stores the project's code and the complete history of changes. It can be local or on a server.
choices: The central storage location for all project files and their history

exercises.question: What is a commit in version control?
exercises.answer: A snapshot of the project at a point in time, with a message describing changes
exercises.explain: A commit saves the current state of files with a message explaining what changed. Commits create the history.
choices: A snapshot of the project at a point in time, with a message describing changes

exercises.question: What is a branch in version control?
exercises.answer: An independent line of development that can be worked on separately from the main code
exercises.explain: Branches let developers work on features without affecting the main branch. Changes can be merged back when ready.
choices: An independent line of development that can be worked on separately from the main code
A copy of the entire repository

exercises.question: What is merging in version control?
exercises.answer: Combining changes from one branch into another
exercises.explain: Merging integrates changes from a feature branch back to the main branch. It can create conflicts if changes overlap.
choices: Combining changes from one branch into another

exercises.question: What is Git?
exercises.answer: A distributed version control system widely used in professional software development
exercises.explain: Git is open-source and tracks changes to files. Each developer has a full copy of the repository history.
choices: A distributed version control system widely used in professional software development

exercises.question: What is a remote repository?
exercises.answer: A central copy of the repository on a server that multiple developers can access
exercises.explain: A remote (like GitHub or GitLab) is a central server. Developers push commits to it and pull updates from it.
choices: A central copy of the repository on a server that multiple developers can access
A copy on a developer's computer

exercises.question: What does 'git push' do?
exercises.answer: Uploads local commits to the remote repository
exercises.explain: Push sends commits from your local machine to the remote server, making them visible to other developers.
choices: Uploads local commits to the remote repository

exercises.question: What does 'git pull' do?
exercises.answer: Downloads and integrates changes from the remote repository into the local branch
exercises.explain: Pull fetches new commits from the remote and merges them into your current branch, keeping you synchronized.
choices: Downloads and integrates changes from the remote repository into the local branch

exercises.question: What is a merge conflict?
exercises.answer: When two branches have incompatible changes to the same lines of code
exercises.explain: Conflicts occur when merging if both branches changed the same code differently. The developer must resolve it manually.
choices: An error in the commit message
When two branches have incompatible changes to the same lines of code

units.title: Testing Levels and Strategies
units.tip: Testing verifies that software works correctly. Different test levels catch different types of bugs. Unit tests check small pieces; integration tests check how pieces work together; end-to-end tests verify complete workflows.

exercises.question: What is a unit test?
exercises.answer: A test that checks a small, isolated piece of code
exercises.explain: Unit tests verify single functions or methods work correctly in isolation, such as a function or class. They are fast and easy to maintain.
choices: A test of the entire application
A test that checks a small, isolated piece of code

exercises.question: What is a test fixture?
exercises.answer: The setup (data, objects) needed to run a test
exercises.explain: Fixtures prepare the test environment. They might create mock objects, initialize databases, or set initial state.
choices: The setup (data, objects) needed to run a test

exercises.question: What is an assertion in a test?
exercises.answer: A statement checking that actual behavior matches expected behavior
exercises.explain: An assertion (e.g., 'assert x == 5') verifies a condition. If it fails, the test fails and reports where.
choices: A statement checking that actual behavior matches expected behavior
A way to skip a test

exercises.question: What is test-driven development (TDD)?
exercises.answer: Writing tests before writing the code they test
exercises.explain: In TDD, you write a failing test first, then write code to make it pass, then refactor. It ensures code is testable and correct.
choices: Writing tests before writing the code they test
Testing only after a bug is found

exercises.question: What is test coverage?
exercises.answer: The percentage of code executed by tests
exercises.explain: Coverage measures how much of the codebase is tested. 100% coverage means every line is tested, though high coverage does not guarantee all bugs are caught.
choices: The percentage of code executed by tests
The time it takes to run tests

exercises.question: What is an integration test?
exercises.answer: A test that checks multiple components working together
exercises.explain: Integration tests verify that different parts of the system (database, API, UI) interact correctly together.
choices: A test of a single function
A test of the entire application from the user's perspective
A test that checks multiple components working together

exercises.question: What is an end-to-end (E2E) test?
exercises.answer: A test of a complete user workflow from start to finish
exercises.explain: E2E tests verify that entire features work correctly. A user logs in, performs actions, and the results are correct.
choices: A test of a complete user workflow from start to finish
A test of a single unit
A test of the database alone

exercises.question: What is a mock object in testing?
exercises.answer: A fake object that simulates the behavior of a real object for testing
exercises.explain: Mocks let you test a unit without depending on external systems (databases, APIs). They simulate expected behavior.
choices: A fake object that simulates the behavior of a real object for testing

exercises.question: What is the test pyramid?
exercises.answer: Many unit tests, fewer integration tests, even fewer E2E tests
exercises.explain: The pyramid shows the ideal balance: lots of fast unit tests (base), some integration tests (middle), and few slow E2E tests (top).
choices: All tests should be E2E tests
Many unit tests, fewer integration tests, even fewer E2E tests

exercises.question: What is a smoke test?
exercises.answer: A quick test to verify basic functionality is not broken
exercises.explain: Smoke tests are fast and shallow; they catch obvious breakage early. They are run before deeper testing.
choices: A quick test to verify basic functionality is not broken

units.title: Code Review and Design Principles
units.tip: Code review is when other developers examine code before it is merged. Good design principles like modularity and low coupling make code easier to understand, test, and change.

exercises.question: What is a code review?
exercises.answer: A process where other developers examine code before it merges into the main branch
exercises.explain: Code reviews catch bugs, improve quality, and share knowledge. They also help keep problematic code from being merged.
choices: A process where other developers examine code before it merges into the main branch
Testing code after it is released
A way to blame someone for bugs
An optional process for open-source only

exercises.question: What is a pull request (PR)?
exercises.answer: A request to merge code changes from one branch into another
exercises.explain: PRs allow developers to propose changes and get feedback, typically reviewed before merging. Reviewers examine the code and approve or request changes.
choices: A request to merge code changes from one branch into another

exercises.question: What should a code reviewer look for?
exercises.answer: Bugs, style violations, design issues, and test coverage
exercises.explain: Reviewers check for correctness, maintainability, performance, and security. They ensure code meets team standards.
choices: Bugs, style violations, design issues, and test coverage

exercises.question: Why is constructive feedback important in code review?
exercises.answer: It helps the developer learn and improves team communication
exercises.explain: Harsh criticism damages morale and creates conflict. Constructive feedback explains issues and offers solutions.
choices: It helps the developer learn and improves team communication

exercises.question: What is a linter in the context of code review?
exercises.answer: A tool that automatically checks code for style and common mistakes
exercises.explain: Linters catch issues like unused variables, inconsistent spacing, and undefined functions before human review.
choices: A tool that automatically checks code for style and common mistakes

exercises.question: What is modularity in software design?
exercises.answer: Breaking code into independent, reusable pieces with clear responsibilities
exercises.explain: Modular code is organized into small, focused units (functions, classes, modules). Each has one clear job.
choices: Writing all code in one large function
Breaking code into independent, reusable pieces with clear responsibilities

exercises.question: What is cohesion in code?
exercises.answer: The degree to which parts of a module are related and focused
exercises.explain: High cohesion means related code is grouped together. Low cohesion means unrelated code is mixed.
choices: The degree to which parts of a module are related and focused
The number of lines in a file

exercises.question: What is coupling in code?
exercises.answer: The degree to which one module depends on another
exercises.explain: High coupling means modules are tightly dependent; changing one requires changing others. Low coupling is better for flexibility.
choices: The degree to which one module depends on another

exercises.question: What is the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)?
exercises.answer: A class or function should have one, and only one, reason to change
exercises.explain: SRP promotes clarity and testing. A function that handles users, saves files, and sends emails violates SRP.
choices: A class or function should have one, and only one, reason to change
Only one person can write code
Code should be as complex as possible

exercises.question: What is the DRY principle (Don't Repeat Yourself)?
exercises.answer: Code logic should exist in one place; avoid duplication
exercises.explain: DRY reduces bugs and makes updates easier. If you copy-paste code, you have violated DRY.
choices: Never use the same variable name twice
No two functions can be similar
Code logic should exist in one place; avoid duplication

units.title: Continuous Integration and Delivery
units.tip: Continuous integration automates testing and merging. Continuous delivery automates deployment. Together, they enable teams to release code frequently with confidence.

exercises.question: What is continuous integration (CI)?
exercises.answer: Automatically testing and integrating code changes multiple times per day
exercises.explain: CI runs tests on every commit to catch bugs early. It prevents integration headaches by catching conflicts early.
choices: Manually testing code once a month
Automatically testing and integrating code changes multiple times per day

exercises.question: What is a CI/CD pipeline?
exercises.answer: An automated sequence of steps to build, test, and deploy code
exercises.explain: A pipeline runs on every code change: compile, test, lint, deploy. It ensures quality and speed.
choices: An automated sequence of steps to build, test, and deploy code

exercises.question: What is a build in CI?
exercises.answer: Compiling code and dependencies into an executable or deployable artifact
exercises.explain: A build checks that code compiles correctly. It is the first step in a CI pipeline.
choices: Compiling code and dependencies into an executable or deployable artifact

exercises.question: What is a CI/CD tool?
exercises.answer: Software that automates the build, test, and deployment pipeline
exercises.explain: Tools like GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI, and Travis CI run automated pipelines on code changes.
choices: Software that automates the build, test, and deployment pipeline

exercises.question: What does it mean if a CI build fails?
exercises.answer: Code did not compile or a test failed
exercises.explain: A failing build indicates a problem; the code cannot merge until it is fixed. The developer must fix the issue and push again.
choices: No one can access the code
Code did not compile or a test failed

exercises.question: What is continuous delivery (CD)?
exercises.answer: Code is automatically tested and prepared for deployment, but humans decide when to deploy
exercises.explain: CD automates everything up to production. A human presses the button to release. This is safer for critical systems.
choices: Code is automatically tested and prepared for deployment, but humans decide when to deploy

exercises.question: What is continuous deployment?
exercises.answer: Code is automatically deployed to production after passing all tests
exercises.explain: With continuous deployment, passing tests means automatic release. No human approval needed.
choices: Code is automatically deployed to production after passing all tests

exercises.question: What is a staging environment?
exercises.answer: A production-like environment for testing before deploying to real users
exercises.explain: Staging mimics production. You can test deployments and user workflows without affecting real users.
choices: A production-like environment for testing before deploying to real users
The live environment that real users use

exercises.question: What is blue-green deployment?
exercises.answer: Running two identical production environments and switching traffic to the new one after testing
exercises.explain: Blue (old) and green (new) environments run in parallel. If green fails, switch back to blue immediately.
choices: Deploying different code to each server
Running two identical production environments and switching traffic to the new one after testing
Deploying to two servers at once

exercises.question: What is a canary deployment?
exercises.answer: Deploying to a small percentage of users first, then gradually to everyone
exercises.explain: Canary deployments reduce risk. If the new version breaks, only a few users are affected.
choices: Deploying to a small percentage of users first, then gradually to everyone

units.title: Refactoring, Technical Debt, and Methodology
units.tip: Refactoring improves code without changing behavior. Technical debt accumulates when shortcuts are taken. Agile and waterfall are different approaches to managing change and delivery.

exercises.question: What is refactoring?
exercises.answer: Improving code structure without changing behavior or adding features
exercises.explain: Refactoring makes code cleaner and easier to understand. Good tests help confirm that behavior does not change.
choices: Improving code structure without changing behavior or adding features

exercises.question: What is technical debt?
exercises.answer: Shortcuts or poor decisions that create future maintenance costs
exercises.explain: Debt is taken on when rushing (writing bad code). It accrues interest (more time to fix, more bugs). It must be paid down eventually.
choices: Shortcuts or poor decisions that create future maintenance costs

exercises.question: What is a code smell?
exercises.answer: A surface-level indicator that deeper problems may exist in the code
exercises.explain: Smells are not bugs; they suggest issues: long functions, duplicate code, unclear names. They warrant refactoring.
choices: A surface-level indicator that deeper problems may exist in the code

exercises.question: What is a long method in code review?
exercises.answer: A function that is too long and should be broken into smaller functions
exercises.explain: Long methods are hard to understand and test. They often do too many things and violate the Single Responsibility Principle.
choices: A function that is too long and should be broken into smaller functions

exercises.question: How should technical debt be managed?
exercises.answer: Balance new features with paying down debt through refactoring
exercises.explain: Ignore debt and it compounds. Allocate some time each sprint to refactoring and cleanup.
choices: Balance new features with paying down debt through refactoring

exercises.question: What is the waterfall methodology?
exercises.answer: A linear approach where each phase is completed before the next starts
exercises.explain: Waterfall is sequential: gather all requirements, design completely, code, test. Each phase (requirements, design, development, testing) must finish before starting the next. Changes are costly and late.
choices: A linear approach where each phase is completed before the next starts

exercises.question: What is the agile methodology?
exercises.answer: An iterative approach that delivers software in small increments with frequent feedback
exercises.explain: Agile works in sprints, building small features and getting feedback. Changes are embraced rather than resisted.
choices: An iterative approach that delivers software in small increments with frequent feedback

exercises.question: What is a sprint in agile?
exercises.answer: A fixed time period to complete a set of planned work
exercises.explain: Sprints are time-boxed, usually 1-4 weeks. The team picks work, completes what fits, and reviews what was done.
choices: A fixed time period to complete a set of planned work

exercises.question: What is a sprint review in agile?
exercises.answer: A meeting where the team shows completed work to stakeholders and gathers feedback
exercises.explain: Sprint reviews demo completed features. Stakeholders see progress and give input for future sprints.
choices: A meeting where the team shows completed work to stakeholders and gathers feedback

exercises.question: When is waterfall appropriate instead of agile?
exercises.answer: When requirements are stable, changes are expensive, and predictability is critical
exercises.explain: Waterfall is often used for embedded systems, medical devices, or aerospace, where changes are costly and requirements are fixed.
choices: When requirements are stable, changes are expensive, and predictability is critical
